title: De altitudine columnarum sub proprio pondere corruentium

deep.reconstruction:
Problem: find the greatest height h at which a uniform prismatic column can stand under its own weight before it buckles. The previous page fixes the model. x is measured from the top. The deflection y vanishes at both ends, x=0 and x=h. The coefficient g is fixed by g·h = ∫_0^h y dx, so g is the mean deflection; times the weight per unit length, it is the horizontal end reaction that keeps moments balanced. This is therefore a column hinged at both ends and loaded only by its weight. The bending equation is m y'' = ∫_0^x (y(s) − y(x)) ds − g x, which differentiates to m y''' + x y' = −g, with m = EI/w (length^3). Its power-series solutions are p = Σ (−1)^k [1·4·…(3k−2)] x^{3k+1}/((3k+1)! m^k) and q (the particular solution belonging to g, starting −x^3/(6m)). This gives y = αp + gq. The conditions y(h)=0 and g h = α∫p + g∫q lead to the buckling condition h p − p∫q + q∫p = 0.

On this page Euler makes everything dimensionless by setting t = h^3/m. Then p = hP(t), q = −Q(t), ∫p dx = h^2 P'(t) and ∫q dx = −h Q'(t). P, P', Q and Q' are entire power series in t (1F2-type hypergeometric series, expressible through Bessel functions of order ±1/3 and ±2/3). The condition becomes h^2 (P + PQ' − QP') = 0, so F(t) = P + PQ' − QP' = 0 involves only the pure number t. Hence h = (m t)^{1/3} = (bb·e·t)^{1/3}, where bb is the cross-section ('amplitudo') and EI = b^4 e, so m = bb·e. Conclusion: for one material, the critical heights vary as the cube root of the cross-sectional area. For similar sections that is the 2/3 power of the diameter, matching the theorem appended to the preceding dissertation. §30 begins listing the four series to be evaluated, and the next page says t must be found by trial and is fairly large.

Check: I evaluated the series at t = 18.57 and got P ≈ 0.4555, P' ≈ 0.3753, Q ≈ 1.9387, Q' ≈ 0.5974. These give F ≈ 0.4555 + 0.2721 − 0.7277 ≈ −5·10^-5, i.e. a root at t ≈ 18.57. This is exactly the accepted modern critical value w l^3/EI ≈ 18.57 for a heavy column hinged at both ends (the clamped-free case is Greenhill's 7.837). Euler's model, series and reduction on this page are therefore correct.
errors: Print says heights follow 'rationem subtriplicatam altitudinum'. By the formula h = (bb·e·t)^{1/3} it must be 'amplitudinum' (cube root of the cross-section); 'altitudinum' is a slip.
Print appears to give ∫p dx = −h²·P'. Consistency with the final equation h²P + h²PQ' − h²QP' = 0 and with the definition of P' in §30 requires +h²P'; the minus is a misprint.
On the next page the third term of Q' has denominator '1……10'; it should be 2……10.
Euler's letter h (height) is rendered as b in the transcription, colliding with bb (cross-section). The formula is h = ∛(m t) = ∛(bb e t), not 't = ∛(bbet)'.

ideas.what: Reduction of the self-weight buckling condition to a single transcendental equation F(t)=0 in the dimensionless load t = h^3 w/EI, via power series in x^3
ideas.modern_name: Heavy column buckling (Greenhill problem), characteristic equation in hypergeometric/Bessel series
ideas.usually_credited_to: Greenhill 1881 (clamped-free, Bessel functions); hinged-hinged case usually to Dinnik / Willers / Timoshenko (20th c.)
ideas.where_published: E510 (this paper); Euler's other 1778 column papers in the same volume; discussed by Truesdell (1960), with details of his verdict unsure

ideas.what: Scaling law: critical height ∝ (EI/w)^{1/3}, i.e. ∝ (cross-section)^{1/3} ∝ diameter^{2/3}
ideas.modern_name: Elastic-similarity height–diameter law (tree allometry h ∝ d^{2/3})
ideas.usually_credited_to: Greenhill 1881; popularised in biology by McMahon 1973
ideas.where_published: E510 and the theorem appended to the preceding 1778 column dissertation

ideas.what: Treatment of the hinged-hinged heavy column, with the end reaction expressed through the mean deflection g = (1/h)∫y dx
ideas.modern_name: Pinned-pinned column under distributed axial self-weight (critical q l^3/EI ≈ 18.57)

missed.claim: The characteristic equation P + PQ' − QP' = 0 is correct for the heavy column hinged at both ends; its root is t ≈ 18.57, the accepted modern value. Engineering literature credits this case to 20th-century authors, not to Euler. Whether Euler's own trial computation on the following pages reached ≈18.6 must be checked there; either way the correct equation is Euler's.
missed.quote: P + P Q' − Q P' = 0, quae aequatio nullam aliam literam inuoluit nisi t
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It corrects priority for the pinned-pinned self-weight buckling coefficient and tempers any blanket view that Euler's 1778 heavy-column work was simply wrong.

missed.claim: Euler states that the critical height scales as the cube root of the cross-section (diameter^{2/3}), a century before Greenhill. Biomechanics (McMahon's elastic similarity of trees) cites Greenhill as the origin.
missed.quote: pro variis amplitudinibus columnarum maximae altitudines quaesitae sequuntur rationem subtriplicatam
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It is a priority point for the h ∝ d^{2/3} allometric law used in plant biomechanics.

deep.surprise_reason: The page itself is a routine nondimensionalisation. However, the numerical check shows Euler's equation is correct and gives the modern 18.57 coefficient for the hinged heavy column. This case and the 2/3-power scaling are usually credited to later authors, though historians such as Truesdell have likely discussed this paper.

't [?] = ∛(bbet)' should read 'h = ∛(m t), hoc est h = ∛(bb e t)'.
∫p dx = h²(½ − …) = h²·P' (the printed minus sign is a misprint).
'rationem subtriplicatam altitudinum' is as printed, but should be 'amplitudinum'.
